name: Phone neck habit change

card.summary: Changing how you hold and look at your phone to reduce 'text neck'; research links the posture to neck pain, but nothing tests facial or neck asymmetry.
card.aka: Text neck habit change, tech neck
card.note: Text neck studies are mostly cross-sectional surveys; causation and appearance effects are not established.

quick.overview:
Text neck is the term for the head-down, flexed-neck posture adopted while using phones and tablets. Phone neck habit change refers to altering that behaviour, for example how long and in what posture devices are used, in the hope of reducing neck strain and, in looksmaxxing framing, neck asymmetry.

Published work on text neck concerns neck pain and posture, mostly in surveys and biomechanical models. None has measured effects on neck or facial asymmetry.
quick.mechanism: Biomechanical modelling shows neck flexion loads the cervical spine joints. Observational studies associate text neck posture and heavy phone use with neck pain in adolescents and young adults, though the link is not uniform.
quick.risks: Behaviour change itself carries little risk. The evidence base is mainly cross-sectional, so cause and effect, and whether altering habits changes appearance, are unestablished.

lead: Text neck is a popular name for the flexed head-and-neck posture used with phones and computers, and a cluster of symptoms attributed to it, mostly neck pain [1][2]. Phone neck habit change describes changing how and how long people use devices to lessen that posture. In looksmaxxing discussion the aim is often stated as reducing neck or upper-body asymmetry.

Researchers have studied text neck in children, adolescents, university students and adults, generally finding associations between text-neck posture or device use and neck pain, although authors caution that the evidence is largely observational [1][3][4][5][6][7]. Biomechanical modelling of neck flexion has quantified joint loading across the cervical spine [8].
No study found has examined whether phone-use habits cause or change facial or neck asymmetry.
infobox: Sustained neck flexion with phones and screens
Mostly cross-sectional surveys, models, case reports

paras: A review of text neck syndrome in children and adolescents describes new technologies shifting neck pain prevalence toward younger ages, and links early and inappropriate use of computers and especially mobile phones to a cluster of symptoms called text neck syndrome [1]. A 2022 review characterises it as a new epidemic needing disentangling, and other papers describe it as an adverse postural phenomenon or question whether it is an epidemic [2][9][10].

A cross-sectional study of 150 young adults aged 18 to 21 in Rio de Janeiro investigated whether text neck was associated with neck pain [3]. A 2021 study in the journal Spine examined the association between text neck and neck pain in adults [4]. A study of university students in Saudi Arabia during the COVID-19 pandemic examined text neck posture, smartphone addiction and neck disorders [5], and a 2023 paper examined musculoskeletal symptoms from phone and backpack postures in school-aged children [6].

A modelling study of eight healthy men quantified cervical joint loads in flexion [8]. A 2022 case report described preventing progression of text neck in a young man [7]. No studies found testing whether changing phone habits alters neck or facial asymmetry.
The entry was added for the idea of reducing neck asymmetry through changing phone posture. No forum material was reviewed for this article, so community claims are not documented here.
